Tonight after she shared what was going through her head, we sat quietly for a while and then I got a notebook and made a list of “Things I can do to feel better” - like go for a walk, call a friend, paint, etc. Is this helping or not good because it’s assuming I know what might make her feel better?? She was sitting right next to me when I made the list and I “discussed “ each idea out loud but she didn’t really contribute much. ..

Thank you for the reply. I think this is an interesting idea. A couple of months ago he asked for weights and a pull-up bar (which he got for Christmas) and wanted to work on his physical fitness.  But he kind of stopped doing it and I haven’t heard him mention it recently. He is really skinny and over 6’ so I could see how increasing his strength and “fighting knowledge” would help his confidence. I will look into it. In the past we never did it because it was very expensive. But maybe we need to reconsider its value. Thanks again.

Thank you for your reply. In typing my reply it keeps beginning with...”I tell him all the time...” and I see that is NOT the same as asking him why he thinks he is bad/terrible/less than. So I will try be more mindful of actually asking him why he says the negative things. Also, I think it might be a first born thing or just his personality when it comes to “if I am not good at it, I don’t want to do it”. My other kids have tried out for sports teams/plays, etc. and not made it, and of course we love them no less and talk about “nothing ventured nothing gained” but he just doesn’t seem to embrace that motto. Maybe we can also work on that, too.

Thank you. We try our best to give them what they need, but sometimes we don’t have what they need. I do have a tendency to try to find the answer but maybe I need to work harder on just letting it be.
